channel.title: Michael Alisky — Travel Newsletter
channel.description: Dispatches from the road: essays, photos, and updates.

item.title: July 22: Shaolin (Poor Kids)
item.content:encoded:
Dear all,

I don't have much to say about Shaolin Temple, except that it's incredibly commercialized and kind of sad. 7 million tourists descend upon Shaolin a year, and at any given moment, approximately 120,000 people are here training in Kung Fu. At the birthplace of Zen Buddhism and Chinese martial arts, several patrons excitedly asked for my autograph, mistaking me for 7'4 French basketball phenom Victor Wembanyama, who underwent a spiritual journey through 10 days of training here earlier this summer.

After a tiring hike, we stumbled across a group of young trainees on an evening run. Their counselor, a monk on a scooter, chased after them, yelling, faster! (快一点). It seemed amusing at first until we saw a literal three-year-old among the group, crying as his little feet pitter-pattered upon the stones. Yes, you read that right: children as young as three board here to begin their kung fu educations. I have to imagine these kids end up emotionally stunted, or maybe just very enlightened. Maybe they're the same thing. Who knows.

From what I gathered, it seems basically like child abuse. I guess it's the price to pay to create kids so astonishingly flexible; they were seriously stretchy.

Oh, and as of a few days ago, the head abbot/CEO monk of the temple was placed under criminal investigation for suspected embezzlement and improper relationships with women. Go figure.

My favorite part of the visit to Zhengzhou was climbing up to the Dharma Cave, emerging drenched in sweat and possibly a bit wiser. It was in this cave that Bodhidharma, the Indian monk credited with founding Chan (Zen) Buddhism, meditated facing a wall for nine years in silent retreat during the 5th century (but if I don't leave my room for a week, it's called depression... go figure). The cave remains a quiet, austere spot nestled high in the cliffs above the temple complex, except someone has placed a bunch of water bottles and gimcracks in the entryway.

I wonder if perfected action comes from repeated training, or more from achieving the right mindset. I'm reminded of this passage from the Zhuangzi:

Yan Hui said, May I ask what is the fasting of the mind?

Confucius said, You must concentrate your attention. Do not listen with your ears, but with your mind; do not comprehend with your mind, but with your vital energy. Your ears can only hear and your mind can only comprehend. But the vital energy is an emptiness that is responsive to anything. The mighty Tao can only gather in an emptiness and that emptiness is the fasting of the mind.

Yan Hui said, Before I learned about the fasting of the mind, I had been conscious of myself. Now… I am no longer conscious of myself. Can this be called emptiness?

Confucius said, Absolutely right...

— Chapter 4 (Watson Translation)

I also liked the nearby Zhongyue Daoist temple, which unlike the Shaolin grounds below, seemed to serve patrons who were genuinely there to worship. While terms like “religion” carry baggage in the post-Mao era, the older language of ritual and faith remains quietly embedded in everyday life. Even self-professed atheists reflexively pause to burn incense or bow three times before passing the main hall.

State-sanctioned temples like Zhongyue occupy a curious middle ground, functioning at once as sites of devotion and instruments of cultural policy. This sign at Zhongyue outlines Xi Jinping thought on the Sinocization of religion, encouraging domestic religious groups to resist domination by foreign forces.

At any rate, I think this little guy really has wu wei (无为) figured out.

That's all for now. Until next time,

Michael

item.title: July 9: Slightly “Ili”-egal Activities
item.content:encoded:
Dear all,

First, hello.

Second, I spent the last few nights in a tent on the roof of a building in Yining, the capital city of Ili region in Xinjiang. “Hammer,” the owner of the wonderful “hostel” we stayed in, proudly told me about the history of the Sibe (Xibe) ethnic minority over a glass of yogurt. He also showed us his homemade Tibetan Buddhist shrine/exercise facility and warned that, if the police asked, we were to say we were sleeping in a nearby park. Sounds good, Hammer!

The Sibe, one of China's officially recognized 55 minority groups, have been living in the Ili region since 1764, when thousands of soldiers and families were forced to relocate here from northeast China to guard the Qing empire's borders.

According to Stanford historian (and rare-typewriter enthusiast) Thomas Mullaney, the number 55 emerged from the ambitious Ethnic Classification Project of the 1950s, during which government researchers attempted to whittle down the 400-or-so distinct ethnic labels that citizens had provided in the nation's first census that had asked, What are you? Some of those answers ranged from major ethnic groups like Han or Manchu to hyper-localized place names like I am from that river over there. Consolidating this bewildering diversity of responses into a streamlined system that was legible and therefore manageable was no easy task, and the reusltant taxonomy continues to shape how the modern Chinese state understands and manages its multicultural population.

Hammer's showers were unfortunately unusable, as somebody had recently cleaned them with a potent combination of bleach and vinegar (NaClO + CH3COOH → Cl2 + H2O + CH3COONa), but the atmosphere at the nearby Liuxingjie shopping district was even more intoxicating than the homemade chlorine gas. Old folks danced, vendors haggled, and onlookers held their breaths as a soccer match being streamed on a big screen went to penalties.

At a nearby Kazakh-style hot pot spot, we accidentally ate horse meat and were again pulled up to dance in front of the entire restaurant.

Celo, Dhruv, Fiona, and I also stumbled into a Russian folk village, where we looked for pastries but instead found some cute little kids who excitedly guided us to a nearby restaurant to meet a local Russian man, Yuri. In fluent Russian and halting Chinese, Yuri explained that his grandfather had moved to Xinjiang as a soldier during the region's Soviet occupation in the 1930s, and his family had stayed.

Like the Sibe, Russians in China constitute an official ethnic minority, with around 15,000 of them in total, mostly living in Xinjiang and Heilongjiang. If I had to guess, there's probably about ten times that many Russian tourists currently partying in techno clubs and wearing Adidas tracksuits throughout China as well. The other day back in Beijing, I even met a few middle school students from Moscow participating in the RICH Chinese Summer Camp (though I'm not entirely sure what the program is actually teaching them).

Yili is famous for its lavender fields, and luckily they were in full bloom.

As the sun set outside the small village of Huocheng, we met a kind farmer, Ma, who saw us walking along the side of the road and gave us a ride to a nearby restaurant. We talked for about three hours, and the restaurant owner later insisted on driving us back to the yurt where we spent the night.

We also visited Lake Sayram, known as the last tear of the Atlantic, skipping rocks and inexplicably becoming very wet.

This sign says not to swim, but thankfully, we befriended some local police officers who lent me their jacket for a quick photo.

Some of us got a little sleepy after that...

At Khorgos, Dhruv and I accidentally crossed into Kazakhstan, realizing our error immediately when a driver blew through a crosswalk and almost hit us. My angry Chinese was met with equally furious Russian. The only other highlights were a museum on Chinese history and a delicious Kazakh food court. I wanted to come here because Khorgos serves as one of the world's largest dry ports, a bustling gateway connecting Kazakhstan and China by rail and highway. Strategically positioned at a gauge break where freight must be transloaded between China's standard gauge and Kazakhstan's wider Soviet-era tracks, Khorgos has transformed from a modest transit point into a dynamic industrial cluster offering value-added services, product assembly, e-commerce fulfillment, and Putin-themed ice cream.

That's all for now! I'm back in the pullulating metropolis of Beijing, missing my friends dearly. Special thanks to Dhruv and Fiona for many of these excellent photos!

Until next time,
Michael

item.title: July 6: Turbulence in Turpan
item.content:encoded:
Greetings and good tidings from Turpan! I've been feeling awfully tubercular lately, like a meek Victorian child stuck in a Gothic sanatorium. To clarify, I briefly fell ill with a minor cold but have since recovered. On the bright side, I think fleeting discomforts like these can help men better empathize with the pains and travails of childbirth. At any rate, with my phlegm expectorated and spirits lifted, I humbly present my latest dispatch:

While off-roading in the Kumtag Desert, predictably, I became violently carsick. Things started off fine but escalated quickly when I asked our driver to turn the music up. We soon found ourselves in a scene straight out of Mad Max, EDM pounding and sand geysering as we launched over successive dunes with increasing abandon. Celo shouted, Witness me! and my stomach swapped places with my liver.

Hours later, as I battled nausea at a Shanshan county rest stop, a 30-car police brigade suddenly thundered by. It was July 5th, the 16th anniversary of the 2009 Urumqi riots, and the state was here to remind everyone of its clout. 45 minutes later, Abu, our driver, received a call instructing us to pull over. Three Uyghur police officers inspected our phones, even checking the recently deleted folder, to make sure we hadn't taken any photos or videos. Thankfully, they overlooked my album entitled Idiotic but political memes, and with the crisis averted, we were soon on our way.

Turpan, one of China's hottest and lowest regions, brims with archaeological wonders, from ancient cities swallowed by sand to lush vineyards defying the arid climate. Pilgrims often travel here to bury their legs in scorching sands, believing the convalescence can heal rheumatoid arthritis, hypertension, and ligma.

Outside the city, we found the ruins of a centuries-old Christian church, built before Islam had made it to Xinjiang.

Celo, Fiona, Dhruv, and I ventured through the famed Karez canals, one of China's three ancient engineering marvels, constructed over 1,000 years ago to channel mountain snowmelt into agricultural fields. I met a garrulous Kazakh gentleman whose views on contemporary race relations, like the subterranean water, were largely unfiltered.

At Jiaohe, a 2,300-year-old earthen settlement and former capital of the Cheshi kingdom, I convinced Dhruv to try cold green bean juice, which he did not like, and we also saw some geese following around a duck.

At a lively local bazaar, Fiona held a Peking duck while Celo munched on lamb skewers, and Dhruv was soon invited to dance.

The nearby Tuyuk (Tuyugou) village, named for an old Yemeni phrase meaning lost the rope, truly felt like a point of no return as temperatures soared beyond 40°C. My favorite part was the Wild Pigeon Home, constructed by a Qing Dynasty carpenter skilled in mimicking pigeon calls. I really love pigeons, so I was happy to overhear a young tour guide explain to some other tourists that pigeons are not only auspicious birds (吉祥鸟), but they also symbolize freedom and peace and exemplify the harmonious coexistence between humans and nature. Right on.

This is our guide Tahir, whom I hired after exchanging a few lapidary Xiaohongshu DMs, and also a photo of me holding a melon.

Tahir was an exceptional guide: knowledgeable, kind, and sincere. He briefly studied English in Xi'an after middle school but had to return home early amid village gossip that he had run away from his wife and middle school sweetheart, Gulmarzhan. After showing us around Turpan and Grape Valley for three days, Tahir graciously invited us over to his home for dinner.

His wife prepared homemade Laghman noodles and served rose-petal tea with fresh jujubes, one of the best beverages I've ever tasted (and a nice change from the aforementioned green bean juice).

At the Bezeklik Thousand Buddha Caves, I developed an intense dislike for Albert von Le Coq, the German wine-merchant-turned-amateur-archaeologist responsible for vandalizing the ancient frescoes and stealing most of the local art.

Finally, this is Wan Dou (豌豆), the resident golden retriever from our Turpan hostel, and also a very cute baby from our uneventful flight to Ili (you can respond to this email with any name ideas).

Thank you for reading, and until next time,
Michael

item.title: July 2: Kashgar to Karakoram
item.content:encoded:
A more detailed version of this dispatch will be made available once I'm back in the states.

Somewhere over the Taklamakan Desert, a sibilant-voiced stewardess handed out cups of buckwheat tea. The onscreen entertainment, which had hitherto consisted entirely of the cooking channel, came to an end, and as we descended into Kashgar, someone offered me green figs. Outside of Xinjiang's second-largest airport, electric cars and horse-drawn buggies bespattered with rustic mire shared the tree-lined speedway. Kashgar is closer to Baghdad than Beijing, but all of China uses one time zone, so at 8:30 PM, the sun would not set for another two hours.

I chatted with the owner of my hotel, who moved here thirty years ago from Sichuan. Like many of the regions Han Chinese, she came to Xinjiang during Jiang Zemins “Open Up the West” 西部大开发 campaign, which began in 1999. This strategy aimed to develop western and interior regions of the country by boosting socio-economic conditions, improving weak infrastructure, and implementing better relations with ethnic minorities.

Many of the Han people I talked to discussed how, before they came to Xinjiang, their families had nothing to eat, but now they lived good lives. For them, Xinjiang represented not just opportunity, but an escape from destitution and unimaginable poverty. Another guest interrupted our conversation to ask the front desk to borrow the hotel's communal nail clippers, which I learned is apparently a thing in China.

The next morning, my driver, Yinqiang, picked me up bright and early at 9 AM. I found him after posting an advertisement on Xiaohongshu, a social media app designed primarily for teenage girls, and we quickly negotiated a rate, route, and trip playlist (the latter consisted almost entirely of Dao Lang). Yinqiang was born in Yili, but like the hotel owner, his native homeland is Sichuan. He told me he doesn't speak Uyghur, but he knows every insult.

Yinqiang started working at age 14 as a tailor, earning between 100-120 yuan per month (or $110–140 in todays USD). As we drove, we talked about his life, family, and goals. When I asked him what the biggest problem facing China today was, he laughed. There are no problems in China! When I asked about Xinjiangs heavy police presence and surveillance infrastructure, he shrugged. Xinjiang is the safest place in China!

Outside Kashgar, the landscape quickly changed, from red mountains to gray glacier-fed rivers, from verdant valleys and turquoise lakes to Aeolian dunes. The formidable Pamirs were the last mountain range on earth to be mapped, and driving through them, I can see why.

The Karakoram Highway was built by China and Pakistan from 1959 to 1979, and it's incredibly smooth and well-maintained. Officially, the road was constructed to promote trade and friendship, but some Indian defense experts have argued its true purpose was to allow rapid military movement or even serve as an invasion route into the Indian subcontinent. Along the way, we met lots of domestic tourists driving RVs decked out with Chinese flags and donning culturally-questionable dreadlocks.

Every hour or so, we stopped for yet another passport check, and also once because there were some police officers handing out free tea (its a funny play on words in Chinese). While I groaned about all the cameras, Yinqiang flashed a toothy grin: its only bad if you're a wanted criminal (通缉犯)!

Here you can see the Muztagh Ata, a massive gneiss-covered dome known as the Father of Ice Mountains in Tajik (one of my nicknames in high school). At the base of this mighty mountain, I learned that I receive a warmer reception here telling people I'm Russian rather than American, as someone immediately treated me to yak meat skewer and exclaimed, я тебя люблю! (I love you!). As an interesting side note, from 1934 to 1942, Xinjiang functioned as a de facto Soviet client state ruled by a local warlord, and from 1944 to 1949, the Soviet Union even backed a separatist regime in the province's north.

Eventually, we reached Tashkurgan, the westernmost town in China, tucked into the Pamir plateau near the borders of Tajikistan and Pakistan. Some scholars believe this is the site of the legendary “Stone Tower” mentioned by Ptolemy in his Geography, the halfway point between Europe and China, where Silk Road travelers paused to rest and trade. The name Tashkurgan itself means “Stone Fortress” in Tajik, and the ruins of that fort still rest atop a bedrock outcrop overlooking the town. Going back over 2,000 years, local kings used the fortress to levy taxes on passing traders, offering protection and caravanserais (temporary lodging) in return.

Today, the city boasts a lively outdoor plaza where locals practice Tajik dance and eat yak meat hot pot. We saw far more Uyghur police officers than I was expecting to see. At The Hunza Kitchen Pakistani restaurant, staff greeted me in Wakhi, a language spoken by an ethnic minority living across the Pamirs in Tajikistan, Afghanistan, Pakistan, and China. They were very pleased to learn that not only does Palo Alto have a Pakistani restaurant (Zareens), but it's one of our most popular spots!

The next morning, Yinqiang and I drove further west toward the Khunjerab Pass, which is 5,000 meters above sea level. Despite my pleas, police officers stopped us about 2 kilometers from the border, informing me that foreigners are not allowed to go any further. I bought some tea eggs and shared them with a stray dog. Hélas.

We took a different route back to Kashgar, at one point driving through the Panlong “Dragon Spine ancient road, an impossibly circuitous ribbon of asphalt clinging to the mountainside with blue fingernails. As he weaved in out of lanes to pass other drivers, Yinqiang's anger rose proportionately to how expensive the other cars were. How can you drive a Land Cruiser and still be scared of the road?" he muttered before swerving past a shiny SUV with Zhejiang license plates.

At the Karakol Lake, I met a young Kyrgyz man, Ardakbek, who proudly displayed his American-style belt. He asked which UFC fighters I liked best and was very disappointed when I couldn't name a single one. One day, I want to go to Texas to see the cowboys! he exclaimed. We also talked about Kobe Bryant and the Los Angeles Lakers, but we eventually got onto heavier topics. He asked me if I knew what America did to the Native Americans. Shocked that he had brought this up, I nodded my head. Of course I know about that, I responded. Most Americans think it's a very dark part of our history. I asked whether he saw any similarities to China's treatment of minorities in Xinjiang, and he shook his head. "What Japan did to us (referring to the Japanese invasion of China in the 1930s)," he said, "that is what America did to its Native peoples."

We departed but soon stopped to buy more apricots and pick black mulberries from the side of the road. Yinqiang bought a truly inordinate amount of yak meat jerky, like at least 20 or 30 bags. At one point, he pulled me aside to whisper: “potatoes are called yang yu (洋芋；foreign tuber) in Xinjiang,” as if it were some kind of secret. We departed, and he promised if I ever came back to Xinjiang, we could become friends and go out drinking together.

Back in Kashgar, I met up with my dear friends Marcelo and Fiona, and we wandered through what remains of the old town. Kashgar used to be one of the best-preserved Islamic cities in Central Asia, a 2,000-year-old warren of winding lanes, clay-brick homes, and sunbaked teahouses. But starting in 2009, the Chinese government began a program of “renovation and reconstruction," citing seismic risk after the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake in Sichuan. By 2014, an estimated 85% of the Old City had been razed and rebuilt. Sterile concrete buildings now simulate the original mud-brick aesthetic, only now, they have better plumbing and built-in mounts for surveilance cameras.

Signs implored residents to "please speak the national language," but I don't think they even need to ask. The kids we interacted with, regardless of their ethnicity, mostly preferred speaking Chinese, and I learned that Uyghur isn't really taught in schools anymore. Virtually all of the locals we met thought Marcelo was Uyghur and that Fiona, his girlfriend, was the most beautiful woman they had ever seen. I think Celo walked with a little more spring in his step after hearing that.

The city's mosques felt like “museumized versions of living culture” as opposed to active places of worship.

Even at the Afaq Khoja Mausoleum, one of the holiest Muslim sites in Xinjiang, we saw no pilgrims but did for some reason find many ostriches.

At 10 AM one morning, we went to the Kashgar city gate to watch a traditional Uyghur musical performance, but the performers' microphones weren't actually plugged in. Under the beating sun and through the throngs of people and sea of selfie sticks, what we saw looked like Kashgar and sounded like Kashgar, but mostly felt like someone was selling a sanitized version of Kashgar back to us.

I hope the censors who read my email are lazy and didn't make it this far, but at any rate, I've used my best judgment. As always, thanks so much for reading. This was a complicated but extremely beautiful trip, and I'm so grateful for the kindness and warmth that everybody we met displayed. If you're interested in learning more about the region or my time here, I'm happy to talk offline or recommend some resources. Expect one more newsletter about Xinjiang soon, featuring Dhruv!

Until next time,
Michael

item.title: June 26: Dandelion Dispatch
item.content:encoded:
Below are a few photos from an overnight train ride from Shanghai to Beijing (shenanigans not included).

After arriving in Beijing, we headed straight for the Dandelion school, a non-profit educational facility serving China's domestic migrant children. Thanks to China's hukou (household registration) system, one's place of birth determines access to public services, including education, healthcare, and housing. Among China's 71 million migrant children, many recieve little or no schooling at all, and those who do manage to enroll in ordinary public schools face systematic discrimination as teachers divert time and resources toward students who are eligble for middle school entrance exams. This exclusion reflects a broader discourse positioning rural migrants as inherently inferior. Places like Dandelion school have thus become essential empowerment spaces, offering not just education but hope for breaking cycles of exclusion. Today, the school provides quality education and a nurturing environment for over 500 students from low-income migrant families.

Also, I redeemed my last airball imbroglio by hitting a game-winning three pointer in a pickup basketball game.

And here's a few shots of the gang getting a little too rowdy at Haidilao hotpot.

Thanks for reading, and until next time

Michael

item.title: June 22: Hanging out in Hangzhou
item.content:encoded:
水光潋滟晴方好，山色空蒙雨亦奇。

“The shimmering water in sunlight is lovely; the hazy mountains in rain are also marvelous.”

— Su Shi (苏轼)

At 6am, Rahul and I took a walk around the fog-adorned Xihu, or West Lake. We reflected on life, love, and Stanford, and we saw many old people and a few Douyin influencers. I think old people have it pretty good in China. They hang out together, practice tai chi, play cards, and gossip. Ninety percent of China's elderly receive care at home, compared with three percent in nursing homes and sevent percent in community-level assistance facilities. As we chatted with a few garrulous old men, the hazy mountains around Xihu were indeed marvelous in the rain.

Xihu is the crown jewel of Hangzhou, a UNESCO World Heritage site that has inspired poets and painters for over a thousand years, and part of the reason why Marco Polo once called Hangzhou the finest and most splendid city in the world. I can only imagine what he might have said if he had seen Aurora, Colorado.

In the old town, our group decked out in traditional (and culturally appropriate) Peking Opera-style (jingju) makeup. I was Zhou Que, a cunning and treacherous villain, which I thought was fitting since people here really like it when I refer to myself as yang guizi (foreign devil).

Kevin also bought a turtle and gifted it to a small child.

At the Doo Crafts factory (the name could probably be better), we watched employees apply tape to boxes with mesmerizing, rhythmic precision. It was as if Butcher Ding had traded his cleaver for tape dispensers and ox carcasses for DIY bead kits:

Cook Ting was cutting up an ox for Lord Wen-hui. As every touch of his hand, every heave of his shoulder, every move of his feet, every thrust of his knee — zip! zoop! He slithered the knife along with a zing, and all was in perfect rhythm, as though he were performing the dance of the Mulberry Grove or keeping time to the Ching-shou music.

— Zhuangzi, Chapter 3 (Watson Translation)

Also, as a reward for making it this far in my newsletter, please have a sausage.

Our last night in Hangzhou was spent at Gongyan, an immersive performance set during the Song Dynasty that told the story of Su Dongpo (Su Shi), a poet, statesman, and once-governor of Hangzhou. It began with his marriage and quiet domestic happiness, followed by the death of his wife and his exile from court (just like my freshman year at Stanford). Snow began to fall indoors. A single line of poetry pierced the silence:

十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。

“Ten years of life and death, both so vast and unclear; without thinking of you, it's still impossible to forget.”

— Su Shi, To the Tune of River All Red

Shoutout to Zane and Fei for these great photos.

It was wonderful to get to catch up with my friend Max over a bowl of green Mapo Tofu. My tongue was numbed and my heart was filled. Thanks for showing me around Zhejiang University!

Also at a tea farm in the outskirts of Hangzhou, I met a nice cat and roasted fresh Longjing (Dragon Well) tea.

All six types of tea can be made from the same leaf: green, white, yellow, oolong, black, and red. Like most things in life, it all comes down to one's oxidation levels and determination.

The workers were impressed with my technique; they said they had never seen a foreigner as talented or handsome as me. I humbly accepted their praise but turned down a request to name me the town's mayor (I am joking, but village elections in China are surprisingly competitive). I signed a few autographs, shook a few hands, and we departed for Shanghai.

There, I caught up with my friend Yuxuan over dinner and got drinks on a rooftop bar overlooking the Bund.

Earlier that day, I also got scammed at a local market and went to a digital government service center to try to complain.

Its worth noting, the last time I was in Shanghai, I visited the marriage market in Peoples Park, where old people gather to trade resumes of their children, complete with photos, salaries, hukou status, and zodiac signs. One of the matchmaker aunties grabbed me and said, you have nice skin (皮肤, pífū), but I misheard and thought she said you have a nice 屁股 (pìgu). Flustered, but not deterred, I responded 你也不错.

Oh, and at Alibaba headquarters, I think they might have photoshopped this picture of Obama from the 2016 G20 Summit to make him look Asian.

Until next time,
Michael

item.title: June 18: Yi Wu-hoo!
item.content:encoded:
The other day at the Shenzhen Huaqiangbei electronics market, I became a business, man, after I helped two Ugandan traders negotiate down the price of solar-powered surveillance cameras. In return, they warmly promised to take me out for Waragi (moonshine made from bananas) if I'm ever in Kampala.

Spanning 1.45 square kilometers and housing roughly 38,000 businesses, Huaqiangbei is the world's largest electronics market. Vendors huddle inside to sell everything from smartphone components to drones, video games to car radios. In 1980, Deng Xiaoping designated Shenzhen a special economic zone, allowing the city of 30,000 to experiment with export-driven industrialization and free-market capitalism. The year before, three military-industrial factories merged and relocated to Shenzhen, forming the Huaqiang Electronics Company. By the 1980s, concomitant assembly plants began to sprout up nearby, transforming the sleepy fishing village of Shenzhen into a bustling commercial-industrial hub (not a dig; I love both fishing and sleeping). From 1980 to 1984, Shenzhen's GDP grew by an average of 58% per annum (compared to national growth rates of 10%). The city's population today is over 17 million.

As I wandered through the electronic labyrinth, I chatted with vendors and bought a pair of cheap headphones. When I asked one woman how the economy was faring compared to 10 years ago, she laughed. China has been developing continuously and will continue to grow! I asked about Trump, and she waved the question off. I'm not interested in American politics. I just do business!

Another vendor kindly offered to help me apply to Feicheng Wurao [If You Are the One], which is by far my favorite dating show. Essentially, a man presents his life story to 30 women who ask questions and buzz out whenever they become unimpressed, often triggered by details like salary, hobbies, or dating history. When I was in 6th grade, I once sent in an application to ABC's The Bachelor, written from the perspective of my golden retriever, Sally: Long blonde hair. Affectionately described by friends as a bitch. Strangers can't seem to keep their hands off of me.

At Tencent's headquarters, AI researchers discussed the impact of US export controls on domestic chip manufacturing.

At a driver training hub for Huolala, I was struck by Party posters celebrating 两弹一星 (China's first nuclear launch program). Even as a private company, Huolala encourages its drivers to view themselves as part of a broader social mission. During the pandemic, for instance, the company played a crucial part in distributing PPE and hand sanitizer.

We also visited OPPO, a smartphone manufacturing company which holds around 15% of the domestic market. At the company's exercise facilities, I airballed a 3-pointer, badly, and unfortunately, two dozen security cameras and 30 or so employees captured the moment on their phones, imprinting my failure into the digital annals of corporate surveillance forever. There go my dreams of playing for the Guangdong Southern Tigers.

In Guangzhou, we visited a clothing sweatshop, where workers earned around $1,000 a month, much more than I was expecting. Its worth noting that wages have risen dramatically in China since the beginning of economic reforms. We also toured Xiaopengs highly automated EV plant and Yihang, a startup developing autonomous passenger drones. One non-military drone designed for firefighting included a convenient mount to attach a turret! For ... uh ... extinguishing things.

From Guangzhou, we flew to Yiwu aboard a COMAC C919, a Chinese domestically-built regional passenger jet. A flight attendant kindly closed the window shades as we began to descend, maybe to help us sleep, maybe because the airport doubles as a civilian-military facility. We were told not to take photos.

Yiwu boasts no glitzy skylines, no imperial ruins, and honestly, no good dumpling spots (though there's a weirdly good club scene). But in global trade terms, it might be one of the most important cities in the world.

Home to the world's largest wholesale market for small commodities, Yiwu is where the planet shops for costume jewelry, fake watches, phone cases, and toys. The International Trade City houses over 75,000 booths arranged by item category, each operated by someone who knows exactly how many military-grade laser pointers will fit in a 40-foot shipping container, and the cost per unit if you want to buy 10,000.

Yiwu's rise began in the early 1980s when local officials, defying central restrictions on private commerce, built permanent market stalls over a drainage ditch. Today, thousands of traders from around the world do business here, and the city is covered in signage in Russian, Persian, and Arabic. As we left the market, a video proudly proclaimed that Xi Jinping has, to date, mentioned the city 10 times in domestic and international news.

I'm a bit overdue on these newsletters, but I hope you'll forgive me. You can expect a few more soon. As always, thanks for reading.

Michael

item.title: June 17: Graduation to Xiang Gang
item.content:encoded:
On Sunday, I graduated with my master's degree, bade a tearful goodbye to my friends, dropped my parents off at the airport, packed up my room, and rushed to catch a midnight flight to Hong Kong.

I'm currently on a bus to Shenzhen, and the primary emotion I'm feeling right now is eepy. But I'm also overflowing with gratitude and excitement for what's to come. The last five or six years at Stanford are hard to describe, let alone understand, but I feel like I'm heading into the world with a kind of momentum and optimism that have, at times, eluded me. I know things that freshman me wanted to know, and far more things have come to me that I was not wise enough to even know I wanted to know.

As I finally leave, things feel kind of right, and I'm ready to go. I'm more focused, appreciative, and sure of myself than I've ever been before. Part of that comes from the adventure ahead, but mostly it comes from the support and love of my friends and family. I'm sure the sadness of leaving will hit soon, but for now, I feel happy.

Over the last few years, I've faced challenges and heartbreaks, disappointments and consternations. But I've also begun to learn how to use these moments of groundlessness (source), when it feels like the rug has been pulled out from beneath me, as opportunities to reassess and replant my feet with greater conviction. I can choose where I land and move forward on new terms.

At Stanford, I've found people who see me clearly. I've developed my voice and pursued my curiosities. I've traveled the world and read (a lot), and I've learned from some of the best. I've had a lot of fun.

In other news, which will surprise perhaps no one, I'll be in China, mostly in Beijing, until December. I'm slowly warming to the idea of maybe applying for a job at some point. I also hope to get better at salsa dancing.

To that end, dearest readers, please do let me know if you'll be in town, or if you'd like to send me devotions or remunerative gifts, or if you have reading recommendations. I can forward you my shipping address and SWIFT info.

My time in China begins with a research trip alongside my academic advisor, Scott Rozelle, and two dozen Stanford students, including Celo and Rahul. Stay tuned for more updates.

Today started at 5 a.m. when we landed in Hong Kong. After a quick hotel breakfast and a shower, we headed to Hong Kong University, a brick-lined urban rainforest whose compactness belied its proprioceptive height, perched a few hundred meters in the air and revealed now and then by sweeping glimpses of the harbor.

We had lunch with the city's Minister of Treasury, who rattled off Hong Kong's rankings in global financial competitiveness, tax simplicity, and regulatory openness, displaying considerable stamina and lung capacity during his rhodomontade on the city he clearly adores.

Eugene, a local community college lecturer who moonlights as a tour guide, narrated the city's development as we drove through the rain-dappled streets. The clouds hung low, sprinkling intermittently, just enough to remind us of their presence.

In a mall bookstore, I read the first chapter of McCarthy's Blood Meridian before Celo and I set off in search of street food. We settled for sandwiches from 7/11 and hurried back to the bus.

I hope to have more time in the coming weeks to reflect on what it means to leave Stanford, but one thing that needs no distillation is the gratitude I feel for the friends who've been a part of this journey, those whom I was able to find photos of, and otherwise. Thank you.

I also decided to upload my past newsletters to a personal website, which you can now view at www.michaelalisky.com. If you find any bugs or client-side errors, keep them to yourself.

Until next time,
Michael

item.title: April 3: Taiwan Dispatch
item.content:encoded:
Tea tastings, hot springs, karaoke, and koalas.

Greetings, gusto, and good tidings! (US trade policy notwithstanding). I'm finally back on campus and have awoken from a nice nap on the couch. I feel like my dad (but with way less swag).

After the unrelenting inclemencies of the Mongolian steppe, I was grateful to have a few days in Taiwan to just chill. Highlights include: seeing friends, eating delicious vegetarian food, bathing in the Beitou hot springs, nodding my head pretentiously during an oolong tea tasting, belting out Deng Lijun at karaoke, galavanting through night markets, and wandering through rainy streets at night.

I even got to see Hannah, which was epic. We met while studying Chinese in Beijing two summers ago, and she's currently in Taiwan teaching English and saving democracy on a Fullbright scholarship.

I'm so grateful to be able to do crossover episodes with friends from different parts of my life.

My only major disappointment was that the famous Jadeite Cabbage was not on display at the Palace Museum (maybe somebody mistakenly ate it?). The museum is full of treasure and artifacts taken from the Forbidden City in Beijing after the Nationalists fled to Taiwan in 1949. I did like this little guy though.

Nastya, Josie, and I also saw koalas, cool birds, and (ironically) Przewalski's horses at the Taipei zoo. I restrained myself/was restrained from hugging the sloths.

Finally, Rahul and I met Daniel and Struan, two European graduate students at NCCU, in the onsen. Long-time readers will recall my love of hot springs, banyas, and other clothing-free male ablutionary social spaces. We checked out Ningxia, discussed civil society civilly, and had a banter-filled night (they were impressed with my knowledge of British slang). Rahul had the profound reflection that its usually more common to take ones clothes off after grabbing a drink.

Cheers to another fun trip. I'm excited to be back on campus where I can read my silly books, go to class, and sit my white ass down and listen 🗣✍.

Until next time.
Michael

item.title: March 27: Mongolia Adventures
item.content:encoded:
Sand, storms, and sandstorms

Long-time readers, devoted seminarians, cherished financial supporters: I'm currently sitting in Incheon International Airport in South Korea, enjoying a snack from the CU convenience store. I shake my head, and soft, vermillion sand trickles out of my ears.

Yesterday, the city of Ulaanbaatar (UB) declared an emergency weather warning due to extreme gusts of wind and high risks of roofs blowing away. Nevertheless, our flight made it out of Mongolia this morning. I'm exhausted but sad to go. Next stop: Taiwan.

As we entered the Gobi desert on Sunday, our driver, Choi, accidentally veered 10 miles off course into a sandstorm. Dust swallowed the air around us, and the sky turned the color of fermented goat milk. Curling wisps of sand ripped across the long road ahead, and we rubbed dish soap on the car's exterior to protect its paint. A few hundred kilometers south laid the border with China.

Using a compass and intermittent bouts of cell service, we eventually found our Way. The melancholic discography of Lana del Rey, recently named Mongolias 2025 Woman of the Year, and Chois phone announcing sporadic Facetime calls from Cat Face with Heart-Shaped Eyes were the only interruptions to our tense, nervous silence. Boggie, the guide Julia found on Facebook, also occasionally proffered mandarin oranges.

As we neared the Khongoryn Els singing sand dunes, a pair of headlights cut across the darkness. A white Prius, packed with ten or eleven people, answered our prayers. Because we were so late, the entire family whose ger we were staying in had come looking.

Gers, also known as yurts in Turkic languages, evolved to suit nomadic pastoralism and transhumance from winter to summer pastures and back. These movable homes have been used continuously by nomads in Central and Inner Asia for thousands of years. Several generations live together under one roof.

Flocks of sheep spilled over the dusty hills and scattered like the mist, and we rode ponies across the Mongolian steppe. Pujee, who fetched the semi-domesticated animals from across the hill on his dirtbike, told us he enjoys eating horse testicles (when presented the opportunity). He offered a few otherwise really profound bits of wisdom.

We saw yaks and pikas and cinereous vultures as we hiked through ice-filled canyons in the Gurvan Saikhan mountains. In our ger, we burnt saxaul wood, coal, and dried animal dung to stay warm through the night. On Tuesday morning, we woke up to a snowstorm.

Temperatures in the Gobi range from minus 40 to over 104 in Fahrenheit (that's 277 to 313 in Kelvin).

Near the Flaming Cliffs paleontological site, winds shook our car, and grass and sheep dung disappeared, and soon there were no more traces of man or beast. We found dinosaur bones and ran headfirst through winds so strong it felt like skydiving (which I last did under rather inauspicious circumstances in Tracy, CA). Choi asked to take a picture (check his Facebook).

After 10 hours on the road careering between oncoming traffic and potholes, we finally made it back to UB, the city where 50% of Mongolia's 3.4 million people live.

Julia, Serena, Johanna, and I had spent the week before in UB for our MA capstone, where we worked with GerHub, a local NGO, to develop policy advocacy mechanisms and advance recommendations surrounding the president's One Billion Trees Initiative. We met with members of Parliament, local bureaucrats, architects, start-up founders, mining magnates, think tank leaders, and one guy who reminded me of Lord Business from the Lego Movie.

Approximately 60% of UB's urban residents live in unplanned ger districts. Citizens face systemic exclusion from the provision of social services and inadequate infrastructure, including a lack of central heating, running water, and sewage systems, which contributes to enormous, striking inequality. Bilgee, who moved to UB 20 years ago and now runs a hot shower, auto shop, and convenience store, showed us his Bruce Lee posters and shared some fermented milk.

More broadly, defining modernity in Mongolia is a difficult task. Mongolia as a country has only been independent since 1924 and was ruled by an authoritarian regime until 1990. In UB, gers exist alongside highrise buildings, reflecting the poverty of displaced rural Mongolians while also symbolizing continuity and respect for Mongol traditions.

Over beers at an expat restaurant, Bat-Orgil, a young student who founded the New Nomad Institute, argued that Mongolia needs to embrace its nomadic roots in relation to climate adaptation, and later teach those lessons to other nations.

I'm grateful for this adventure and for how much I learned, and I'm optimistic we can contribute something useful toward the many challenges we observed. My favorite moment on the trip probably came at the second ger Julia and I stayed at. Using Google Translate, I asked a young boy how old he was. In English, he confidently answered, 23. I asked him what he liked to do for fun. He thought for a bit before responding: Hold baby goats.

Until next time.
Michael

item.title: December 24: Spanish Study
item.content:encoded:
Merry Christmas, Happy Hanukkah, and a Joyful Kwanzaa to all!!

I'm finally back home, and after a brief hibernation, I wanted to send one final newsletter to cap off my time abroad.

I spent the last week gallivanting through Andalucía, with each dinner starting later and ending more tipsy than the last. In Granada, I met up with my dear friend Abi to visit the Alhambra palace, where we observed all 17 mathematically possible wallpaper groups (unique ways to tile a 2D plane) and learned how medieval hydraulics work. The Alhambra was first built between 1238 and 1358 during the Naṣrid Emirate of Granada's golden age but was nearly lost to ruin until restoration in the 1800s.

At night, we bar-hopped through winding alleys, receiving a complimentary tapita (small appetizer) with each drink — I don't know what it would take to bring this practice to the US, but if you're reading this and are capable of doing something, please do.

I satisfied my yearning for the subaltern in the Sacromonte neighborhood, where whitewashed caves carved into the hillside in the 16th century provided religious and ethnic sanctuary for marginalized groups. Many remained inhabited well into the 20th century. I think I might have seen an amateur Bitcoin mining operation underway in one of them.

In Sevilla, I met up with Alonso, one of Marcelo's friends from Lima, and we ate a pecha (Andaluz for a shit-ton) before catching a Flamenco show at a local tablao.

Alonso also took me to a Semana-Santa-themed bar, an incense-filled Catholic fever dream where the house drink (as far as I could tell, the only cocktail available) is called the Blood of Christ, a crimson concoction of grenadine, sparkling wine, and gin. Someone who knows more about Catholicism will have to comment on how sacrilegious this is.

On the subject of blasphemy, I added a new entry to the historic canon of cantankerous, eccentric Petes: Peter the Great, my little brother, and now, Pedro I of Sevilla. A Christian king, Pedro commissioned his palace, the Alcázar, to replicate the Alhambra. Elaborate Arabic inscriptions still proclaim Glory to the Sultan Don Pedro, and I couldn't find a single cross inside the complex (although there was a Star of David). Pedro, evidently, beefed with the Church and met his untimely end at the hands of his half brother in 1369.

Along with King Pedro, Christopher Columbus is also buried inside the Seville Cathedral.

A short train ride away in Cádiz, I climbed the Cathedral tower, where I met an older German gentleman who informed me he was on a search for ancient ruins. We talked entirely in German, so I really didn’t understand much, but at one point, he tapped his chest and said, “I have Roman blood in my heart.” I wonder how many times he thinks about the Roman empire each week.

In ancient times, Cádiz (then known as Gades) was considered to be located at the edge of the known world. The Latin phrase non plus ultra (nothing further beyond) is associated with the city. They've got great seafood too.

Back in Seville, I got a much-needed haircut and fed some ducks. At night, we hung out at the Alameda de Hércules and grabbed dinner at my friend's friend's girlfriend's aunt's restaurant (buss).

I had a wonderful time in Spain, and it was a great way to cap off an awesome adventure. I've grown during these last few months and learned a lot, and I'm grateful for this extended opportunity. But man did I miss home!

As for these newsletters, that's a wrap! To my friends who read these updates, thank you so much. Your engagement, thoughtful responses, and generous financial contributions have made all the difference.

Until next time,
Michael

item.title: December 4: Georgian Dream
item.content:encoded:
Bulochka and khinkali.

Gamarjoba from the Republic of Georgia! My past week was jam-packed with inspiring, interesting, and heartwarming moments. This is a long email, so I'll get right into it.

As you probably know, over the past six days, tens of thousands of demonstrators have taken to the streets to protest the government's decision to temporarily suspend EU ascension talks. Last week, the ruling party also nominated a pro-Russia ex-football player as their presidential candidate. Meanwhile, despite massive protests, the government passed a Foreign Agents Law in May which expanded their capacity to crack down on pro-democracy groups and NGOs. Finally, the party won a controversial parliamentary election in late October that the EU called neither free nor fair.

On Rustaveli Avenue, protesters wearing raincoats and swim goggles launched fireworks at police officers armed with water cannons. Further back, demonstrators wrapped in Georgian and EU flags blew horns and shone laser pointers. Cheers erupted with each volley of color that exploded against the limestone walls of the parliament.

While some anti-Russian sentiment was visible, the people I met framed their struggle as more of a fight between democracy and tyranny, an unflinching demand for accountability. Outrage against police violence further increased turnout. Someone showed me a video of a police officer kicking an already unconscious woman in the head.

Older folks lamented the ongoing catastrophe, and Shota, who runs a small photography museum in Kutaisi, told me all he wants is peace. He also explained the tension between the country's Christian values and opposition to LGBT+ rights amidst pressure from the EU to reform.

At breakfast this morning, a lively debate ensued between two Greek tourists and a Georgian couple. All four were firmly pro-Trump but had mixed views on Putin. Things quickly escalated when I asked how much Georgia had influenced ancient Greece's culture.

What really made this trip special, though, was meeting my second cousin, Isabella (Belka). She left St. Petersburg a few years ago and now works as an actress and producer in Tbilisi. The last time we saw each other was in Russia when I was two years old. Catching up and hearing her life story was a surreal experience, made all the richer by fresh khachapuri and a liter of semi-sweet red wine. She is truly epic, and it was really special to reconnect.

Belka and I also took a day trip to Kazbegi, a district in northern Georgia nestled in the Caucasus mountains. We visited fortresses, danced at the friendship monument, survived a frozen Marshrutka ride, and tried six types of local honey.

After returning to Tbilisi, Belka's boyfriend joined for dinner (borscht inside a bread bowl…life changing), and I met their dog, Bulka, who is blind, has cancer, and has survived at least three bullet wounds. And yet she still wags her tail.

Bulka was adopted off the streets a few weeks ago. Georgia has more stray dogs than anywhere I've ever been, and they receive tags when the city vaccinates and neuters them. The dogs, for the most part, are big chillers, and they receive color-coded tags based on how friendly they are.

As a crazy side note, we met some Turkish guys near Stepantsminda who told us their Kangal puppy, Maya, was a gift for a good friend in Chechnya.

Back in Tbilisi, my friend Mariami introduced me to her brother Akaki, who took me to a few places with a great view that describe the Georgian character well, including the Father David cemetery, the Chronicles of Georgia Monument, and Sameba cathedral.

I later learned the meaning of "shemomechama" (the food was so good that I couldn't help but overeat) after Akaki ordered 20 khinkali for us to share (words cannot describe how good these were).

On a cloudy day in Mtskheta, Georgia's ancient capital, I visited more monasteries and churches, many of them over 1,500 years old, and listened to polyphonic Orthodox singing.

My trip to Georgia ended in Kutaisi, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Europe, where Jason began his search for the legendary Golden Fleece.

Last night, I found some cows. I walked backwards and attempted to lure them into a cave to no avail, before hiking along railroad tracks from Gelati Cathedral to the Motsameta monastery.

Kutaisis name translates to the city between a stone and a mountain, which is exactly where I found myself after I got lost on my way back. After michvagaling along the highway in the dark for an hour, I eventually managed to catch a ride back to town.

I was out cold as soon as my head hit the pillow, but I awoke when my host knocked on my door at 11pm to offer me a glass of homemade wine.

Before then, though, I have a German exam tomorrow to study for. Wish me luck.

By the way, check out this mummified crocodile and blue hippo from the Kunsthistorisches Museum (well, Egypt technically).

If you've made it this far, thanks for reading.
Until next time,
Michael

item.title: November 25: November News
item.content:encoded:
Mulled wine, time capsules, and San Marino's music scene.

Devoted readers and dearest seminarians; cherished friends and respected foes: I hope you will forgive me for the long delay in our correspondence!

Amidst a dazed stupor, In the middle of the journey of our life, I came to myself within a dark wood where the straight way was lost, and I realized it has been three weeks since my last email. Hélas!

On November 5, during a boisterous election night watch party, my friends and I stayed up late phone banking, as cheers erupted from the MAGA Europeans every time Trump won another battleground state.

Soon thereafter, I made syrniki for Astrids cat, Moritz, before taking the train to Brno, Czechia, in search of two noteworthy attractions: the Brno dragon, hanging in the City Hall, and a suppository-shaped, marble-dispensing astronomical clock located in the towns main square (spoiler: neither were hard to find).

To be fair, if I were a 16th century Czech townsman, I would probably also think this crocodile was a dragon.

At the Vienna Staatsoper, we saw a ballet rendition of The Winter's Tale by Shakespeare, and I then exited to Bratislava, pursued by a bear, for a night of contemporary music and wine from San Marino.

More specifically, the Embassy of the Republic of San Marino hosted a concert in Slovakia in celebration of the 60th birthday of Massimiliano Messieri, one of the major figures, if not THE major figure, of San Marino contemporary music panorama, and you know I had to pull up 🔥 I did fall asleep twice during the concert, but the after party was pretty lit.

A special shout out to this film shop for keeping it reel, even in the digital age.

Until next time,
Michael

item.title: November 5: Slovenia Stories
item.content:encoded:
Dragons, dolines, and dairy.

Hello hello!

This weekend, my friend Laura and I took a bus to Ljubljana, Slovenia, the city of Dragons, founded by Jason and the Argonauts, home to automatic raw milk vending machines.

Non-homogenized, non-pasteurized, and no antibiotics. I went full BadlandsChugs. I definitely regretted that, but at €1 a liter, you really can't beat the price. YOLO.

Ljubljana is pretty, but the real beauty lies outside the city. On Saturday, we rented a car and drove to Lake Bled, a castle-adorned glacial lake located in the Julian Alps. We also found a very picturesque forest cat.

A few miles away in the Triglav National Park, we hiked through the Vintgar Gorge and got lost in the woods after dark. Thankfully, my indefatigable spirit, innate sense of direction, and full access to Google Maps facilitated our safe return.

The next day, we drove to Karst and learned about dolines, sinkholes that form when cave roofs erode away, creating staggering voids in the earth. As a geologic term, doline originates from the Slovenian language. When fog formed, the Big Collapse Doline, pictured below, was thought to be the gate to the underworld.

I yearned for the mines, and Laura and I descended into the Škocjan caves (no pictures allowed). Walking along torch-lit, meandering staircases cut directly into the rock, surrounded by dripping stalactites, it felt like I was traveling through the tunnels of Moria (thankfully, no Balrogs).

After an obligatory Krem cake, we drove to Trieste, Italy, an ancient Roman settlement which eventually became the Austrian empire's main sea port. A syncretism of imperial influences, this Little Vienna on the Sea boasted impressive neoclassical architecture, Habsburg-era coffee houses, and super legit gnocchi. I especially enjoyed hanging out in the Unity of Italy Square and wandering through the narrow lanes of the Jewish Ghetto.

Also, this is the definition of I know a spot.

Back in Ljubljana, we visited the city castle, ate burek, and saw Slavoj Žižek and Melania Trump's alma mater. I stopped by the first pizza restaurant in ex-Yugoslavia.

Slovenia was super stunning, and I'm already planning my next trip to the Balkans!

Also, tonight is the US election, and the only thing scarier than the fact that our country's future rests in the hands of a few voters in rural Pennsylvania, is our award-winning Halloween costume (my head was too big to make the Uncle Fester bald cap work).

Finally, it was so lovely to see the inimitable Sae Kobayashi, all the way from Indonesia!!

Until next time,
Michael

item.title: October 28: Wow, Wachau!!
item.content:encoded:
Christian girl autumn is officially here! And how better to celebrate than with a visit to Schönbrunn Palace, the Hapsburg’s main summer residence? Unfortunately, about 14 separate Chinese tour groups had the exact same idea, and there was a 4-hour wait to get in. We decided to just walk around the gardens instead.

The day before, October 26, was Austrian National Day, a holiday commemorating Austria’s constitutional enshrinement of permanent neutrality in 1955. To celebrate, I woke up early to catch a train to the Wachau valley, a “sundrenched” and “enchanting” gesamtkunstwerk (total work of art) and gathering place for epicures from around the globe” (find someone who talks about you like the Danube River tourism website writes about Wachau).

Wachau was beautiful, spooky, and yes, enchanting. Starting in Krems, we hiked for almost eight hours through golden vineyards and rolling hills along the Danube, stopping at Dürnstein Castle just before sunset. In 1192, Richard the Lionheart was imprisoned here after offending Leopold V of Austria during the Third Crusade. According to legend, his loyal minstrel Blondel discovered the king’s location by singing beneath each castle in the realm until he heard Richard’s voice joining in from within the fortress walls. A similar thing once happened to me while singing “No Flockin’” by Kodak Black in the stacks of Green Library.

We barely made our train back to Vienna and eventually made it home around 11 PM… and promptly went salsa dancing. I was tired, but as Bad Bunny once remarked in a song, Siempre puest[o] pa' la misión.

Speaking of classical music, I had a lovely time at the Italian embassy last week for a concert by a 19-year old piano virtuoso. My favorite piece was the Rachmaninoff Études-Tableaux in C minor.

Today, I also went to the Kenyan Embassy for a conversation on the recent Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC) conference and Africa-China relations more broadly. At least, thats how it was advertised. We ended up talking about different notions of community, Africa-centered international relations, and Africas role in the world more broadly. Interesting discussion!

And it's no Colorado sunset, but the views from the Kenyan embassy were pretty sweet.

Afterward, we cooked burritos in the DA kitchen, which was really nice until Immo informed the group that German men prefer to pee sitting down (when given the choice). Theyre apparently taught that peeing while standing is uncultured/unhygienic. Im still processing the full impact of this disclosure, but I just thought you all should know.

Oh and also! The German word for meerkat is Erdmännchen, which translates directly to little earth man. I quite like that.

Until next time!
Michael

item.title: October 22: Turkey Tales
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday on the way to Istanbul Airport, I asked my taxi driver if we could stop for ice cream. He thought about it, said one minute, and then offered me a cigarette. I declined and took a nap as we inched our way through the traffic. I wonder if he didn’t understand “ice cream,” or if he just thought his gift was preferable.

Part of the reason I was so tired is because when I returned to my hotel room late the night before, there was a cat sitting on my bed. He was friendly enough, and very polite, but I have no idea how he got in.

Yusuf (I decided to call him Yusuf) woke me up a few times during the night, nibbling at my feet or otherwise entreating cuddles. When a nearby mosque announced the morning call to prayer, he meowed to be let out but came back a few hours later to say goodbye as I packed up my room.

Not including Yusuf, Istanbul has over 125,000 stray cats, and they're all remarkably affectionate and clean. Cats are considered ritually pure within Islam, but Istanbul in particular benefited from their presence during Ottoman times, when traditional wood houses and a warm climate facilitated the spread of disease-infested mice and rats.

I met many great cats, and also one asshole cat which deserves special attention for stealing food right off my plate. Unrelated, but this is the Blue Mosque.

With all the important stuff out of the way, I also wanted to write a bit about Istanbul's unique cultural heritage, history, and architecture.

In 482, a man named Petrus Sabbatius was born near modern Skopje, North Macedonia. The son of a pig farmer, by 527, he would eventually become emperor. There's far too much to say about Justinian I in this one email, but I bring him up because his mark on old Constantinople was indelible. Under his rule, the Byzantine empire built the Hagia Sophia and Basilica Cistern, reconquered former territories, and codified Roman law. In 532 Justinian declared an era of perpetual peace with the Sasanian empire (which lasted 8 years). He even managed to smuggle in silkworm eggs from China to establish a domestic Roman silk industry.

The Hagia Sophia was of course the main showstopper. Because the Ottoman rulers removed the church's Christian ornamentation, the central dome almost felt more grand in its emptiness.

Speaking of, I lost track of time while reading on the subway and found myself on the edge of the old Constantinople walls. I walked along them for a few hours, stopping to play soccer, feed pigeons (güvercin), and try boda, a mildly alcoholic drink made of fermented chickpeas.

I eventually reached the Gate of Saint Romanus, where, in 1453, Mehmed the Conqueror besieged Constantinople, transforming the city to Ottoman rule, and with it, turning the Hagia Sophia into a mosque.

These are the Aqueduct of Valens, built in 368, seamlessly incorporating a modern highway underneath.

Thats enough of that for now, but DM me if you want more pictures or facts related to Istanbuls Roman history. I think about it almost daily.

The next day, I explored the Archaeology Museum with Enes and Meva, and afterwards, felt inspired by this poem to climb a walnut tree in Gulhane park.

Across the Bosphorus in Kadıköy, Miray was shocked to hear I hadn't yet tried authentic Turkish baklava, and she ordered 8 different kinds. It was delicious but deeply unfair; Miray promptly told me she was on a diet and that the baklava were for me. It was way too much for me, but as she admonished, no çöp, i.e, no leftovers.

I also tried Tavuk Göğsü, a sort of milk pudding made with shredded chicken breast (not my favorite, but the macros are insane). The texture was like if someone who did not know how to make pancakes tried to make pancakes (looking at you, Peter).

Other highlights include sneaking into a Chinese tour group at Topkapi palace and trying some life-changing white bean stew (Kuru Fasulye) near the Pera Art Museum.

If you've survived my bloviating this long, well done, and thank you. It means a lot to hear my friends are reading and enjoying what I’m writing.

My only extraneous advice is to remember that the royal palace where Atatürk died is called Dolmabahçe, not Domalbahçe, which is an important linguistic distinction.

A huge thank you to Irmak, Fiona, Emre, and Lara for all your recommendations and suggestions in this beautiful city. I’m sad to leave Istanbul, but I’m looking forward to spending some time in Vienna where I can catch up with classes and friends.

Until next time,
Michael

item.title: October 14: Budapest Bangers
item.content:encoded:
Guten Abend, Partymenschen!

I'm currently on a train back to Vienna from Budapest, contemplating many life decisions. Here are some representative stats from the weekend:

  • 64,938 steps
  • 5 total hours of sleep
  • 2 words of Hungarian: Egészségére (cheers) and igen (yes) and 1 Australian dance sequence learned
  • 0 thermal bath chess games (I really tried to make this happen though)
  • and countless missing brain cells

I stayed in a hostel for the first time, which is just like a hotel, except it's way cheaper and also some drunk guy enters your room at 5am singing in Italian. We did get little treasure chests to store our belongings though, which I think complemented the overall experience.

One weekend in Budapest is enough paprika for a lifetime. On Saturday, I met up with Rachel and Zai, two American friends from the DA, for a succulent meal of paprika catfish soup and a side of paprika potatoes. We finished by snorting lines of paprika directly off the table (this is a joke, mom).

“The spice” is indigenous to Central Mexico and only arrived in Hungary in the 16th century through the Balkans (then under Ottoman control). But it wasn't until the 19th century that paprika became a defining feature of Hungarian cuisine and culture, and not until the Soviet occupation that agricultural production really took off. Hungarian scientist Albert Szent-Györgyi even used paprika peppers to isolate the chemical structure of Vitamin C, garnering him the 1937 Nobel prize in Medicine or Physiology.

On the Buda side of Budapest, we tried Lángos, a deep fried flatbread topped with garlic, sour cream, and cheese (this was a hit).

At St. Stephen's cathedral, we found the mummified holy right hand of Hungary's first king, Stephen I, and also the tomb of Ferenc Puskás, a legendary Hungarian footballer who led the Mighty Magyars to a 6-3 victory over England in 1953 (his memorial featured no severed body parts, as far as I could tell).

On the tour, we also befriended two Aussie solo-travelers named Paris and Jovan and spent the day sightseeing together, as well as the night, which began with dinner at a funky industrial style restaurant called Kiosk that my friend Betty recommended, and we finished at a 7-in-1 party death star called Instant-Fogas. Of course, no night out is complete without a pit stop at a karaoke bar.

This weekend was a lovely, spontaneous, sleep-deprived adventure, and I can't wait to explore more of Europe and meet more wonderful people.

Some other recent highlights include a döner with Immo at Ferhat and dessert at Vollpension with Kate and Zai. Vollpension is a coffee house in Vienna that employs sweet old ladies as the bakers and servers. It functions both as a pension supplement and a means of maintaining social interactions for the elderly.10/10, no notes.

To paraphrase a Russian saying, life is good, and to live is also good! I've found a rhythm with my studies (by the way, students knock on the table rather than clapping after lectures here) and I've relished exploring places like the Museum for Applied Art and going for walks in between classes.

Next week, I'm "chucking a sickie" and heading to Istanbul for a long weekend. Until then I'll be hibernating.

Michael

item.title: October 4: Baden Backroads
item.content:encoded:
Week two in Austria has been busy, and I have been müde (tired)! My time here has been filled with impressive art, wandersome adventures, questionable sandwiches, and wonderful new friends.

Last weekend, I took a trip to Baden, a UNESCO World Heritage site known for its Roman baths and Biedermeier culture, where Beethoven composed major parts of his 9th Symphony. One can almost imagine the composer strolling through the town's elegant Art Nouveau villas, humming Ode to Joy while sipping on local wine (still waiting for him to drop the next album).

Our journey was perhaps… a bit less refined… 60+ future diplomats (yours truly included) embarked on a boisterous bacchanal through Baden's famed vineyards, stopping every 20 minutes to try different types of Sturm, a fermented grape juice well on its way to becoming wine. Its important to remember that, much like Sturm, were all just works in progress.

After finally reaching the restaurant some four hours later, we ate a girl dinner (crackers and cheese) with, of course, more wine. All in the name of international relations.

On Tuesday, the school year officially started with an inauguration at the Rathaus, Vienna's City Hall. My main takeaway is that Vienna must be an exceptionally well-run city if taxpayers are willing to fund such bougie office space for their local government.

Also, as a student from Austria informed me, that is indeed the flag of Vienna, not Indonesia.

The event featured a bizarre documentary about the OG sauced up white boy and DA alumni, Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall, and concluded with a speech by Volker Türk, current UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.

After class the other day, I also visited the Belvedere, one of a few palace complexes in Vienna not built by the Hapsburgs (it was the residence of French expat and renowned short king, Eugene of Savoy). In 1955, the museum hosted the signing of the Austrian State Treaty, reestablishing Austria as a sovereign state after World War II.

Other recent highlights include the Museum of Military History, bachata dancing in my room, and this rock, Ivan.

Classes have been great — I'm especially enjoying German, which I'm taking at the A1 level (bloody beginner). On the first day, I told the teacher I liked apples and water, which has naturally resulted in her calling me Apfel Wasser.

I'm also taking a class on the History of Economic Thought and Methodology, which has explored Carl Menger's subjectivism, as well as a China seminar with a professor even more chaotic than Scott Rozelle.

Overall, the vibes are great, and it's so nice to be somewhere where I can walk and think, and think and walk. The people couldn't be nicer, and it's been a real privilege to have so much free time for adventures.

Missing you guys, and until next time,
Michael
